title: Scalable and Adaptive Trust-Region Learning via Projection Convex Hull
claim: An iterative loop initializes, partitions, trains and prunes many simple components, then combines them into one compact final structure.
layout: Top-to-bottom vertical flow with side loop, input top-left, output bottom-left
description: The figure shows a vertical pipeline. At top left, a 3D scatter plot of red positive and blue negative points is labeled as the high-dimensional, large-scale training dataset. An orange arrow labeled 'Hyperplane initialization' leads to a dashed box with Hyperplanes 1 to n, each shown as a small 3D plot with an orange plane. Colored bands and arrows run downward through these steps: a yellow band 'Divide dataset into subregions for each hyperplane' leads to Subregion 1 to n plots. A green band 'Design the loss...' leads to green boxes Loss 1 to n. A blue 'Gradient descent' band leads to updated hyperplanes in a second dashed box. A gray arrow and a 'Renew and iteration' box loop back to the top. A large blue arrow, 'If converge, combine', points to the final convex hull, a blue-shaded polyhedron in a 3D scatter plot at bottom left. Color-coding by stage guides the eye.
caption: Overview of the PCH framework. At each iteration, data are partitioned into subregions assigned to hyperplanes, which are updated by gradient descent on the surrogate objective; hyperplanes are dynamically added or pruned, and the final convex hull is obtained by combining the active hyperplanes.
abstract: Learning compact and reliable convex hulls from data is a fundamental yet challenging problem with broad applications in classification, constraint learning, and decision optimization. We propose Projection Convex Hull (PCH), a scalable framework for learning polyhedral trust regions in high-dimensional spaces. Starting from an exact MINLP formulation, we derive an unconstrained surrogate objective and show that, under suitable weight assignments, the optimal hyperplanes of the MINLP are recovered as stationary points of the surrogate. Building on this theoretical foundation, PCH adaptively constructs and refines hyperplanes by subregion partition, strategic weight assignment, and gradient-based updates, yielding convex hulls that tightly enclose the positive class while excluding negatives. The learned polyhedra can serve as geometric trust regions to enhance selective classification and constraint learning. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that PCH achieves strong performance in accuracy, scalability, and model compactness, outperforming classical geometric algorithms and recent optimization-based approaches, especially in high-dimensional and large-scale settings. These results confirm the value of PCH as a theoretically grounded and practically effective framework for trust-region learning. Codes are available at https://github.com/IDO-Lab/trust-region-pch.
